archetype.name: Game Manager (spot-start backup)
archetype.definition: A nine-year undrafted veteran who wins by staying on schedule, throwing short, and keeping a run-first offense out of trouble, not by pushing the ball downfield.

report.headline: Forty-six ugly dropbacks bought a QB3 seat; the career says he's better than this.
report.take:
Cooper Rush is a career backup whose value has always been competence on short notice: about 6 yards per attempt, completion rates a few points below expectation, and very few sacks. In Dallas he went 4-1 as a spot starter in 2022 and carried a ten-game stretch in 2024 without hurting the team badly. That profile makes him a floor-raiser, not a ceiling-raiser, which is exactly what Atlanta's offense needs. It runs the ball well (2nd in rush EPA), passes about 10% less than game situations predict, and leans on the 1st-ranked run defense in the league.

His 2026 sample is grim and short. He started Week 1 at Pittsburgh, then took 58% of the snaps in relief of Tua Tagovailoa in a 34-3 home loss to Carolina. Across 46 dropbacks he sits 41st of 42 in EPA per dropback and last in interception rate. He threw 4 picks on 39 attempts and took 5 sacks. Since Week 3 Michael Penix Jr. has started, and Rush is now listed as QB3. He was inactive for the Saints game, serving only as the emergency quarterback.

The damage is concentrated, which matters for judging it. Three of his four interceptions came on just 7 throws in the 10-19 yard range, and all four went middle or right. To the left he completed 83% of 12 attempts for positive EPA. Throws under 10 yards were roughly break-even with a 50% success rate. The 62.5% pressure-to-sack rate, about five sacks on eight pressures, is the least believable number here: he ranked 4th, 13th and 2nd in that stat in his previous three charted seasons. What does look real is how conservative he has become. His 7.7% aggressiveness and a target depth five yards short of the sticks are far below the roughly 20% tight-window rate he played with in Dallas. Bijan Robinson, not a receiver, was his top target, at negative EPA per target.

Going forward, the most likely outcome is zero snaps. As QB3 behind Penix he needs two things to go wrong to see the field. If he does, expect the 2022/2024 version: around 6 yards an attempt, slightly negative EPA, and an interception rate well below 10%. That is a passable caretaker for a run-first team, not a reason to project offense.

strengths.title: Historically elite at avoiding sacks
strengths.body: Across three prior charted seasons he turned pressure into sacks at some of the lowest rates in the league. He gets the ball out or throws it away. The 2026 spike rests on about eight pressures and contradicts years of evidence, so it should snap back if he plays again.

strengths.title: Short game holds up
strengths.body: Throws of 0-9 air yards were essentially break-even, with half of them successful, and the left side of the field produced positive EPA. That is the part of his game that fits a run-heavy offense with a top-two rushing attack. It is also the part most likely to repeat.

strengths.title: Spot-start track record
strengths.body: His Dallas stints show a quarterback who can keep a team afloat: 4-1 in 2022 with near-zero EPA, and 12 touchdowns over ten games in 2024. It is a modest résumé, but it is a far larger sample than his 46 dropbacks this year.

concerns.title: Intermediate middle-of-field turnovers
concerns.body: Three interceptions came on seven throws between 10 and 19 yards, and the middle and right of the field produced all four picks. The sample is tiny, but it is the throw a backup has to hit to move the chains. On third down he converted just 15% of the time against an average of 8.5 yards to go.

concerns.title: Accuracy has always lagged
concerns.body: He has posted a negative CPOE in every season on record. The -13.6 this year is an exaggeration of a real trait, not an aberration, and nearly a quarter of his throws were charted as bad throws. Even with regression he is a below-expectation passer, which caps how much he can lift an offense.

concerns.title: Shrinking aggressiveness, shrinking role
concerns.body: He is throwing into tight windows far less than in Dallas, with an intended depth five yards short of the sticks, so even clean games produce little. That conservatism, plus the results, has dropped him to QB3. That role is the biggest limit on his value.

trend.note: A shaky Week 1 start (-15.8 EPA) was followed by a worse relief outing against Carolina (-12.2 EPA on 17 attempts, plus a lost fumble). He has since gone from starter to emergency QB behind Penix.

nextGame.headline: Emergency-only role; Baltimore's short-zone defense would squeeze his checkdowns
nextGame.body:
Rush is QB3 and was inactive last week, so the base case against Baltimore is no snaps. If he were pressed in, the matchup works against his profile. The Ravens are 4th in EPA allowed on short passes, exactly where he lives. They are only 19th against deep throws, which he barely attempts, and the two deep balls he tried this year both fell incomplete. Baltimore's pass defense is 9th overall, while its run defense is 26th. Any Atlanta quarterback would lean on the run game here.

Availability on both sides shapes the game more than it shapes him. Left tackle Jake Matthews, a 100%-snap starter, left the Saints game with a groin injury and is questionable, which would weaken protection for whoever plays quarterback. Baltimore is without edge rusher Trey Hendrickson, and corner Marlon Humphrey is questionable after leaving with a calf injury. Lamar Jackson's ankle is the swing piece: with him, the Ravens' 2nd-ranked passing offense could force Atlanta out of its run-first script.

keyMatchups.title: Checkdowns into a stingy short defense
keyMatchups.body: His intended air yards are just over five, and Baltimore ranks 4th against short passes. If he played, the easy completions that kept him near break-even would be harder to come by. This holds for any game he enters against them.

keyMatchups.title: Atlanta run game vs soft front
keyMatchups.body: Atlanta's 2nd-ranked rushing offense meets the 26th-ranked run defense, which suits a pass-light offense. This is the game script that would protect a backup quarterback if he were needed.

keyMatchups.title: Blindside protection in question
keyMatchups.body: Matthews has played every snap this season and is questionable. Baltimore's pass rush is modest (24th in sack rate) and down Hendrickson, which softens the risk, but a backup tackle would hurt any quarterback.

nextGame.watch: Whether he is active at all: if he is promoted to QB2 or Penix is limited, his role changes overnight.

restOfSeason.body:
As QB3 behind Penix, his expected weekly output is essentially zero, and the useful question is what he looks like if forced into action. Most of this season's line should regress toward his career. The 10% interception rate and 62.5% pressure-to-sack rate come from tiny samples and contradict years of data, so expect those to normalize. The accuracy deficit and the low yards per attempt are real and have been with him every season.

In a spot start behind this run game and defense, a reasonable expectation is a 2022/2024-style line: about 6 yards an attempt, around one turnover, and an offense that wins on the ground if it wins. The conservative passing would cap his production even then.

bets.reason: Atlanta's 2nd-ranked rushing offense faces Baltimore's 26th-ranked run defense, and Atlanta's 1st-ranked run defense limits the Ravens' ground game. Lamar Jackson's ankle adds downside for Baltimore at home-underdog odds of +120. This angle is about the team and has nothing to do with Rush, who projects to be inactive.

confidence.note: 46 dropbacks over two games, now QB3 and likely inactive.
